 Govt must hold firms accountable for haze as S’pore did, says think tank
 17-Nov-2026, 13:59 17 Nov 2026, 13:59 FMT Reporters Share Global Institute for Tomorrow questions Malaysia’s lack of action against companies potentially linked to transboundary haze, citing Singapore’s move to investigate their operations.
 Global Institute for Tomorrow founder Chandran Nair speaking at the 2026 International CEO and Business Leaders Forum in Kuala Lumpur today. 
 KUALA LUMPUR : The government should follow Singapore’s example by investigating companies linked to transboundary haze and holding those responsible accountable, says Global Institute for Tomorrow founder Chandran Nair. 
 Nair criticised what he described as Malaysia’s failure to take meaningful action against businesses whose operations may have contributed to the recurring environmental crisis.
 Pointing to Singapore’s recent move to summon business leaders over possible links to forest fires in Indonesia, he asked why Malaysian authorities had not taken similar steps.
 “That is what governments are meant to do, but in Malaysia, not one company has been (identified) by the government, brought in and talked to.
 “(Do) you think we don’t operate in Indonesia?” he said at the 2026 International CEO and Business Leaders Forum here today.
 On Oct 23, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said it had sought documents and information from 10 Singapore-registered companies regarding their links to businesses in Indonesia, their land concessions and the measures they had taken to prevent or combat fires.
 Senior Singapore ministers subsequently met representatives of the companies and demanded full cooperation with investigations, including access to information on their operations, supply chains and corporate relationships.
 The Singapore government stressed that the exercise was aimed at establishing responsibility rather than presuming the companies had engaged in any wrongdoing.
 Nair said the haze problem had persisted for decades, arguing that business leadership and ethical commitments must be backed by effective regulation and enforcement.
 “We need rule of law. We need regulations. We need enforcement,” he said.
 He urged business leaders to be intellectually honest and allow science and economic policies to guide their decisions.
 The latest transboundary haze episode affected air quality in Malaysia for more than two months, beginning on Aug 8 and continuing well into October, with authorities attributing the pollution to forest and land fires in Indonesia’s Kalimantan and Sumatra regions.
 Conditions were particularly severe in Serian, Sarawak, where the air pollutant index (API) soared to 521 on Sept 4, far exceeding the hazardous threshold of 300. The deteriorating air quality prompted an emergency declaration and forced the closure of schools in parts of the state.
 On Oct 28, natural resources and environmental sustainability minister Arthur Joseph Kurup told the Dewan Rakyat that the government had examined allegations involving Malaysian-linked plantation companies but found no conclusive evidence that they were responsible for fires in Indonesia.
 He said any party found to be responsible would face appropriate legal action, while acknowledging the challenges of obtaining evidence from overseas and establishing corporate liability.
